page_summary:
Lawrence Sutin's Divine Invasions: A Life of Philip K. Dick (Harmony, 1989; revised Carroll & Graf, 2005) is the foundational full-length biography of Philip K. Dick and the source-of-record for nearly all post-1989 secondary scholarship's biographical claims. At 554 pages it remains the longest treatment of the life. Sutin's project depended on the cooperation of Paul Williams (the Estate's literary executor and editor of the PKDS Newsletter) and on extensive original interviewing — Anne Dick, Tessa Dick, K.W. Jeter, Tim Powers, James Blaylock, Doris Sauter, Russell Galen, and many others sat for him. The book emerged when industry insiders had declared a PKD biography commercially impossible; Sutin credits agent Dorothy Pittman for marketing it and editor Michael Pietsch for buying it.

Method: Sutin's reportorial method is the book's distinctive contribution. Where contemporaneous testimony exists he uses it; where Dick's self-reports are unverifiable he flags them as such; where accounts diverge he records the divergence rather than adjudicating between them. The result is a biography unusually durable as a source: subsequent scholars who disagree with Sutin (Anne Dick, Rickman, Arnold) are working against a record clear enough to disagree with. Sutin organizes the life chronologically across seventeen chapters, weights the major creative periods (the Point Reyes years, the post-divorce drug period, the post-2-3-74 Exegesis years) in proportion to their biographical density, and ends with a measured chapter on the meaning of the visions that explicitly refuses to settle them.

Contributions to PKD studies: (1) the canonical biographical timeline — dates, addresses, marriage chronologies, drug-use sequences, publication histories — that all later scholarship cites; (2) the corpus of original interview testimony, especially from spouses, friends, and editors no longer available to scholars working after 1989; (3) the methodological model of reportorial neutrality on the contested events (the break-in, 2-3-74, the Vancouver episode); (4) the framing of PKD as a serious American writer whose life warrants biography on the same terms as a literary novelist's, not as a special case for science-fiction commemoration; (5) two editorial volumes that complement the biography — In Pursuit of VALIS: Selections from the Exegesis (Underwood-Miller, 1991) and The Shifting Realities of Philip K. Dick (Pantheon, 1995) — together with Divine Invasions these constitute the foundational triad of secondary Dick.

Position in the literature: Anne Dick's The Search for Philip K. Dick (1995) is the most direct response, contesting Sutin specifically on the 1959–1965 Point Reyes period and the marriage's collapse. Gregg Rickman's Philip K. Dick: In His Own Words (1984), preceding Sutin, gives the unfiltered late spoken self-commentary; Rickman's later To the High Castle (1989) treats the early years at greater depth than Sutin compresses them to. Kyle Arnold's The Divine Madness (2016) reads the visions clinically where Sutin reports them neutrally. Anthony Peake's A Life of Philip K. Dick (2013) gives the visions a more permissive frame than Sutin allows. Each successor biography presupposes Sutin and works in some specific relation to his account; he remains the field's biographical baseline.

Fan reception: the book also functioned as the entry-point reference for non-academic readers, and Sutin's tone — sympathetic without being reverent, source-attentive without being dry — set the register for the post-1989 wave of fan-press writing on Dick (Bruce Gillespie's editorial work, the PKDS Newsletter, later PKD Otaku). The fan and academic receptions converged on Sutin's authority more than on any other single secondary text.

Caveats: Sutin's coverage of the Exegesis predates the 2011 Lethem/Jackson published edition, so his reading of the text is necessarily partial — he saw the manuscript in CSU Fullerton's archive but could not assume any reader would. The 1959–1965 Point Reyes period is contested by Anne Dick on specific grounds. The Vancouver episode and the late drug-use chronology are contested by Rickman. The 2005 revised edition addresses some but not all of these.

## To my good and loving parents, Jack and Rochelle Sutin 

3 

## **ACKNOWLEDGMENTS** 

The research and writing of this book proved to be an adventure beyond all initial expectations. Those who regard Philip K. Dick’s probings into “What is Real?” as mere metaphysical quibblings have never undertaken to write a full account of a life. 

I am indebted to so many persons who extended me time and consideration that it seems ungrateful to single out a few for special thanks. But I must mention those whose support was most vital. My agent, Dorothy Pittman, diligently marketed my proposal at a time when those “in the know” declared that a biography of Philip K. Dick was a commercial impossibility. Dorothy was also, for me, the perfect readerone who dreams along with the text. My editor, Michael Pietsch, took the risk of purchasing the book and, in his labors on the manuscript, respected my style and intentions while constantly spurring me to greater clarity and depth. Paul Williams, the literary executor of the Philip K. Dick Estate, provided all the cooperation a biographer could ask for; his sole concern was that, insofar as possible, the truth be told. Anne Dick gave vital support by granting me numerous long interview sessions and access to her excellent book Search for Philip K. Dick. Tessa Dick, Nancy Hackett, and Kleo Mini all graciously responded to my interview queries on their married lives with Phil. Laura Coehlo and Isa Hackett, Phil’s daughters, similarly extended their cooperation. Tim Powers, Phil’s good and true friend, unstintingly shared his memories, journals, and personal contacts. Joseph Morris, my good and true friend, shared the vision of this book with me throughout. 

I interviewed well over one hundred persons who knew Phil or possessed information about him, and I thank all who-out of love and respect for Phil-took the time to talk or write to me. A few of these persons shall, by their own wishes, go nameless here. All errors and omissions in the text are, of course, solely my responsibility. But I can extend my most heartfelt thanks to: Gerald Ackerman, Karen and Poul Anderson, D. Scott Apel, Alexandra Apostolides, Chris and Greg Arena, Lawrence Ashmead,
